notes.b: After the Famine, Irish agriculture shifted towards cattle, dairy and sheep, and the stronger farmers grew in number and wealth.
points: Tillage declined as a share of agricultural output, while the livestock sector, especially cattle for export to Britain, expanded in the 1850s and 1860s.
Rising prices for livestock and dairy products from the 1850s improved the position of larger farmers, who could buy more land and equipment.
The number of small holdings fell after the Famine, and holdings were consolidated into larger farms.
The stronger farmer class gained influence in local life and in the politics of the Tenant League and later movements.
Labourers and small tenants remained poor, and many relied on seasonal work or on emigration to find an income.

notes.b: Emigration continued in large numbers, and its patterns shaped the economy and the families left behind.
points: Emigration after 1850 was dominated by young single people, and many went to the United States, Britain, Canada and Australia.
Chain migration meant that families and neighbours who had gone abroad sent passage money and information back to Ireland, encouraging others to follow.
Remittances from emigrants sustained many families who stayed, and they paid for farms, dowries and the passage of relatives.
Emigration reduced the surplus labour supply and helped to keep wages and land prices higher than they might otherwise have been.
The detailed treatment of emigration, including the diaspora's political and social role, is covered in the notes on the Irish diaspora.

notes.h: The national school system and education
notes.b: The national school system, established in 1831, expanded after the Famine and became the main provider of primary education.
points: The national school system was set up in 1831 under the Stanley Letter, which offered government grants to schools that admitted children of all denominations.
Its aim was to provide a non-denominational education, with religious instruction taught separately by the churches.
The system was opposed by the Catholic hierarchy, which wanted denominational control, and many Catholic schools continued to be run by the Church.
The Christian Brothers, founded by Edmund Ignatius Rice, ran schools that taught large numbers of boys in the towns and expanded in the 1850s and 1860s.
The Queen's Colleges, established in Belfast, Cork and Galway in 1845, were non-denominational colleges that the Catholic hierarchy condemned.
The Catholic University of Ireland was founded in Dublin in 1854 under John Henry Newman, who was its first rector.
Attendance at national schools and literacy rates rose after the Famine, and the decline of the Irish language was reinforced by the English-language curriculum.

notes.b: The railway network was built from the 1830s and expanded rapidly after the Famine, changing trade, towns and communications.
points: The Dublin and Kingstown Railway, opened in 1834, was the first railway in Ireland and ran from Westland Row in Dublin to Kingstown.
William Dargan, the contractor who built much of the Dublin and Kingstown line, went on to build railways across Ireland and to lead major public projects.
The network expanded in the 1840s and 1850s, and by 1870 Ireland had a railway network of roughly 1,800 miles (about).
Railways reduced the cost of moving cattle, grain and passengers, and they opened inland markets to the livestock trade.
Railways encouraged the growth of towns such as Athlone and Portarlington, which became railway junctions, and drew trade away from older ports.
The railway network also made travel to Dublin and to the ports easier, which helped the flow of emigrants to Liverpool and other ports.

notes.b: Dargan was the leading Irish railway contractor of the period, and his projects showed what private enterprise and public patronage could achieve.
points: William Dargan was born in County Carlow in 1799, and he began as a labourer and then a contractor on road and canal work.
He built large sections of the Dublin and Kingstown Railway, and he later became the leading railway contractor in Ireland and Britain.
He was the central figure in the 1853 Great Industrial Exhibition in Dublin, which he financed and organised, and which drew large crowds.
Dargan was a witness and participant in the transformation of Irish transport after the Famine, and his firm built much of the main railway network.
Contemporaries admired his entrepreneurial success and his philanthropy, and he gave large sums to public causes, including the Exhibition.
Later historians have judged him as a symbol of the Irish businessman who achieved success within the British economic system, while noting the limits of his role in Irish industrial development.

notes.b: Belfast developed differently from the rest of Ireland, with linen, engineering and shipbuilding, and a rapidly growing population.
points: Belfast's linen industry expanded after mechanisation of spinning and weaving in the 1820s and 1830s, and it became the centre of the Irish linen trade.
Engineering works grew in the city alongside linen, and foundries and machine shops supplied the textile mills.
Edward Harland and Gustav Wolff established their shipbuilding firm in Belfast in 1861, and it became the city's leading shipyard.
Belfast's population grew rapidly after 1850, with migrants arriving from the rural counties of Ulster and from the Famine-affected west.
The city's sectarian geography was marked, with Protestant and Catholic communities concentrated in different districts, and riots broke out in the 1850s and 1860s.
The region's development was based on capital, skilled labour and links with Britain, which set it apart from the largely agricultural rest of Ireland.

notes.b: The dowry system and late marriage reflected the importance of land and inheritance after the Famine.
points: Marriage was often delayed until a farmer could provide a dowry for the bride, and late marriage became common among both men and women.
Dowries were paid in cash or land, and they were often used to secure a farm for a son and to provide for the daughters who stayed.
A large number of people never married, especially in the west, and the delay in marriage contributed to falling birth rates.

keyTerms.definition: A sum of money or land paid by a bride's family on marriage, which after the Famine was a key condition of marriage and the inheritance of farms.
The continued system of landlord control of estates after 1850, in which estates changed hands through sales and the new owners often managed land more commercially.
The non-denominational primary school system established in 1831, which received government grants and became the main provider of primary education.
The pattern in which emigrants sent money and information home that encouraged family members and neighbours to follow them abroad.
The non-denominational colleges established at Belfast, Cork and Galway in 1845, which the Catholic hierarchy condemned.
A farmer with a substantial holding who was the most prosperous tenant in the countryside and gained influence after the Famine.
